# Tank and combined-arms warfare (`tank_combined_arms`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs internal_combustion_engine; helped by electromagnetic_waves_radio, machine_gun, military_aviation, general_staff_war_college
- Core idea: The First World War tank brought tracks, armour and a combustion engine together in a vehicle able to cross some forms of broken ground. Early machines were slow, mechanically unreliable and demanding to supply. At Cambrai in 1917 and Amiens in 1918, tanks took part in battles involving infantry, artillery and aircraft. Combining different arms was an ancient practice. Engines and radio changed how quickly commanders could coordinate them. The 1940 campaign in France illustrates the consequences of differences in organisation and communications even when both sides possess substantial armoured forces.
- Pitfalls:
  - Believing Germany won in 1940 with more or better tanks; the Allies fielded many tanks, including armoured divisions; organisation, communications and command decisions contributed to the outcome
  - 'Blitzkrieg' was not an official German doctrine but a later label
  - Tanks without infantry are destroyed in towns and woods; range varies by vehicle and terrain, and shortages of fuel or spare parts can immobilise a formation
  - Early tanks broke down more often than they were knocked out
- History: greece: 4th c. BC – Alexander combines phalanx, light troops and cavalry (ancient combined arms); europe: c. 1487 – Leonardo's sketch of an armoured car (unworkable); 1916 – first tanks at Flers-Courcelette; 1917 – massed tanks at Cambrai; 1918 – Amiens, tanks with artillery, infantry and aircraft; 1920s–1930s – theories of Fuller, Tukhachevsky and Guderian; 1940 – fall of France; global: 1939–1945 – armoured combined-arms formations decide land campaigns from Poland to Manchuria
- Read:
  - Jonathan M. House, Combined Arms Warfare in the Twentieth Century (2001)
  - Karl-Heinz Frieser, The Blitzkrieg Legend: The 1940 Campaign in the West (2005)
